title: How often does a short window of sound sync real phones and cameras to within a video frame, and can a confidence set in one room hold in another?
lede: research programme: audio sync of free-running cameras and phones on real devices; step 1 runs on five real smartphones recording the same speech in a 200 ms and an 800 ms room (LibriWASN, 20 sessions): their clocks differ by 0 to 19 ppm (median 13.7, stable within about 1 ppm across sessions, under half the 40 ppm earlier projects assumed); with -10 dB of added white noise a 2 s window misses by more than a frame 17% (200 ms room) and 34% (800 ms room) of the time with GCC-PHAT, but 5% and 7% with partial whitening (gamma 0.25), so PHAT is the worst weighting in real rooms too, against our simulated-room result; the peak-to-sidelobe ratio flags failures well (AUROC 0.91 to 0.998 for 2 s windows), but a gate set in the drier room lets 3.7% of 2 s windows through wrong in the wetter one at -10 dB, against the 1% it was set for
summary: An open research programme (track 13, capture) on syncing free-running cameras and phones from their own sound: how often a short window fixes the offset to within one 30 fps frame on real devices, rooms and clocks, and whether a confidence calibrated in one room or rig keeps its failure rate in another. Step 1 (2026-11-13) runs on LibriWASN (Schmalenstroeer, Gburrek and Haeb-Umbach 2023; Zenodo, CC BY 4.0): five smartphones (Nexus, Pixel 6a, two Pixel 6, Pixel 7, Xiaomi) recording the same loudspeaker playback of LibriSpeech, 10 ten-minute sessions in a room with about 200 ms and 10 in one with about 800 ms of reverberation. Only the phone channels are fetched, by HTTP range requests, and none is committed. For each of the 200 phone pairs a reference line (20 s GCC windows every 10 s, Theil-Sen) is checked without ground truth: every pair kept at least 97% of its windows within 5 ms of the line, and the three lines of every phone triple add up to within 1.8 ms (median 0.3 to 0.5 ms), far under the 33 ms frame. The phones' sampling clocks differ by up to 19.1 ppm (median 13.7 ppm), the same within about 1 ppm from session to session and room to room. Short windows (0.5 to 4 s, 40 seeded times per pair and session, a simulated start-offset prior of ±1 s because the published files are pre-aligned) were scored for five weightings, with the recordings as published and with independent white noise added at 0 and −10 dB. With added noise, PHAT is the worst weighting in both real rooms and partial whitening (gamma 0.25 to 0) the best: at −10 dB, 2 s windows fail 16.9% and 33.6% of the time with PHAT against 5.0% and 7.2% with gamma 0.25 (95% session-bootstrap intervals separate), which reverses capture-reverbsync's finding in simulated rooms. The 800 ms room is harder than the 200 ms one at −10 dB, as predicted. As recorded, PHAT still fails 3.3% of 2 s windows in the 200 ms room (spread over all ten pairs at scattered wrong lags, cause open; gamma 0.25 removes nearly all of it) against a predicted under 1%. The peak-to-sidelobe ratio separates good from bad windows (AUROC 0.91 to 0.998 at 2 s), but a threshold set in one room to let at most 1% of accepted windows be wrong, applied in the other, holds on average over noise levels (0.6% to 1.6%) and not at −10 dB from the drier to the wetter room (3.7% for gamma 0.25, 5.5% for PHAT). Limits: one dataset, one loudspeaker playback of read speech, white rather than real noise, simulated start offsets, phones not cameras; the reference's own error (closure up to 1.8 ms) bounds sub-ms claims.
